summary: AC5 as amended by ADR-0026 is implemented, and the central design premise checks out against the production code. 24 blocking producers x one 1000-record chunk each puts ~4.9-5.3 MB of serialised segment in the accumulator per ceiling interval (SegmentWriter.encodeRun emits CODEC_NONE, so the highly compressible 'x'.repeat(180) payload is NOT squeezed away and the fillRatio argument survives), i.e. ~0.58-0.63 -- Accumulator.adaptInterval's else branch, the only regime that HOLDS currentInterval. The 8 MiB size trigger is not reached (Accumulator.estimatedFramedBytes gives ~5.26 MB against 8.39 MB, 1.6x margin). The warm-up is genuinely required (Accumulator.java:56 starts at intervalFloor; the else branch at 174-177 leaves it untouched) and correct: drain #1 sets lowStreakStartMillis, the jump is lengthenDelay+5s, drain #2 sees the streak satisfied and jumps to the ceiling. WarpableClock is sound -- the offset never moves after warm-up, and only millis()/instant() are consumed. The files/s arithmetic is right (LocalFsBinStore = data + .v sidecar per object; SegmentPublisher PUT + CommitLog.putIfAbsent = 2 objects = 4 files/flush; 16 files/s at the floor vs 0.8 at the ceiling), and both the >2s probe and the <4 files/s check are robustly satisfied on the passing path with no flakiness risk I can find. The Gradle task is correct: 900s JUnit @Timeout inside a 20min task timeout, JaCoCo off, 256m, isFailOnNoMatchingTests. Separating it from memoryBoundTest is right for a reason stronger than the budget one given -- running both in one JVM would let the first test's heap state pollute the second's peak sample. The producer harness is concurrency-clean: ready.countDown() is the first statement so ready.await() cannot deadlock, AssertionError from the in-thread 202 check lands in failures, and written uses addAndGet (M1.18's set would have been wrong here). SKIP=check-tdd is the honest handling: tdd_scan.task_for derives the Gradle task purely from the /src/<sourceSet>/java/ path segment and tdd-red.sh has no override channel, so nothing on gate-design rungs 1-5 was reachable inside this task's scope; M0.38 correctly names the rung-3 fix, and task_for is already pure and unit-testable so that fix is cheap. Cost lens: no production change, and the test's own assertion is on flushes per second, not on records -- the right direction. Five minors, none blocking. Two small imprecisions I am NOT filing because they err conservatively: the true fillRatio is ~0.58 rather than the ~0.62 the javadoc states, and the safe band is ~17-37 producers rather than the ~16-34 it states; both move the figure further from 0.9, so the conclusion is unaffected.

findings.finding: The files/s assertion does not catch what its comment says it catches. The comment claims '⚠️ This is what catches the case where fillRatio strayed above 0.9 and adaptInterval shortened back to the floor mid-run', but the assertion is an AVERAGE over the whole load, and total file count is roughly regime-independent -- the same 24 blocking producers contribute one ~5.2 MB batch per flush whether the interval is 250ms or 5s, so ~152 files are written either way and only the elapsed time changes. If the shortening happens after fraction f of the data, files/s is about 152 / (9.6 + 182.4f), which is below the 4.0 threshold for any f greater than about 0.16. A shortening at the literal halfway point gives ~1.5 files/s and passes. What the check DOES catch is the systematic case (fillRatio above 0.9 from the very first flush -- e.g. PRODUCERS raised to 38 or the pad enlarged), which is the more likely bug, so the assertion is worth keeping; the word 'mid-run' is the false part. The same sentence is repeated verbatim in docs/internal/product/backlog.md:198.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change grows the serialised per-record cost (a wider directory entry, a bigger pad, an added field) so that fillRatio crosses 0.9 a third of the way into the run. adaptInterval shortens to the floor on that drain, the remaining two thirds of the 200 MB stream at the 250ms regime, files/s comes out around 1.5, the test passes, and the backlog row and M3/VERIFIED continue to claim NFR-6 was proven with the interval held at its ceiling when for most of the run it was not.

findings.finding: Two Thread.sleep(300) calls in the warm-up violate testing.md rule 15 ('No Thread.sleep. Inject a clock.'), and the reason given for them is not true. The comment says 'the background flusher polls on REAL time, so it needs a moment to drain each warm-up append before the clock jumps out from under it.' The drain is already guaranteed without the sleep: sendTinyBulk blocks on the 202, BulkService sends the 202 only after appendBulkBody returns, that returns only after Ingest.append's mine.done().join() completes, and DefaultIngest.flushLocked completes those futures only after Accumulator.drain() -- and therefore adaptInterval, and therefore lowStreakStartMillis -- has already run. So the sleeps are dead weight resting on a false premise, in a test that otherwise takes care to derive its timing from config rather than from wall-clock luck.
findings.failure_scenario: A future editor trusts the comment, concludes the warm-up is timing-sensitive, and either widens the sleeps when the test is slow on a loaded machine (masking a real regression behind a longer wait) or copies the sleep-then-jump pattern into a test where the 202 does not carry the same durability guarantee -- at which point the clock jump really can land before the drain, lowStreakStartMillis is never set, the interval never lengthens, and the copied test silently measures the 250ms floor while claiming the ceiling.

findings.finding: Scratch goes to the system temp directory, against testing.md rule 17 ('Scratch under build/tmp, never the system temp directory'), and roughly 200 MB of segment files, commit deltas and .v sidecars is left behind on every invocation -- @AfterEach stop() only stops the WebServer, and nothing deletes the tree created by Files.createTempDirectory("binstore-memflat-ceiling"). MemoryFlatUnderTenXBodySizeTest has the identical deviation so this is copied rather than invented, but it doubles the tree's exposure, and this is the task more likely to be run repeatedly while its producer count or timings are being tuned.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer runs ./gradlew :http:memoryBoundCeilingTest a dozen times while tuning, /tmp accumulates ~2.4 GB (on WSL2, whose disk pressure build.md already calls out), and the next run fails inside LocalFsBinStore.put with ENOSPC. That surfaces to the test as an IOException mapped to 503, so the failure reads as 'a producer failed' or 'the store rejected a chunk' rather than 'the disk is full', and the first hour is spent looking at the ingest path.

findings.finding: The new row backfills an ID below the current maximum. backlog.md's own header states 'IDs are stable and never reused'; M0.38 has never been issued so this is not literally a reuse, but the highest allocated M0 ID in the file is M0.51 and the new row takes M0.38 out of the M0.34-M0.37 gap region. AGENTS.md:269 records that at least one ID from exactly that gap (M0.37) was spoken in conversation across a whole session and never written down, which is why the gap exists.
findings.failure_scenario: An earlier or concurrent session that spoke 'M0.38' for a different piece of harness work writes it down later, or a future agent allocates from the same gap. Two unrelated tasks then share one ID, check-commit-msg.sh accepts commits for both because it only checks that the ID appears in the file, and the backlog stops being a resolvable index -- the exact defect the AGENTS.md 'Never' bullet about unresolvable IDs was written to prevent, one step worse because both entries resolve to something.

findings.finding: The new comment says 'M3.5 adds MemoryFlatAtIntervalCeilingTest as the SAME tier, excluded and wired the same way: the reasoning above applies unchanged', and the paragraph it points at claims the tier is run 'on demand plus CI'. The CI half is not true today: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only ./gradlew dependencyLicenses and pre-commit run --all-files, and neither memoryBoundTest nor memoryBoundCeilingTest appears there or in check. Wiring CI would be scope widening for this task and the sibling is in the same position, so this is about the claim, not the omission -- but AC5's evidence now rests entirely on one manual run recorded in a backlog row, and the comment reads as though a machine will re-run it.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone refactors the accumulator or the bulk chunking, runs ./gradlew check and CI, sees green, and ships a change that makes memory grow with the interval. Nothing re-runs the 200-second proof, so the regression is found only when a later milestone happens to invoke the task by hand -- or in production, which is what NFR-6 exists to prevent.
